prompt: A team moves its file server to cloud storage and argues that nothing changes for security, since the provider guards the building. Which difference does that argument miss?
hint: Where are the controls now, and who can reach them?

choices.text: The provider reads every file it stores, so confidentiality is gone
choices.why: Nothing in the course says that; the provider's half is done well. The change is on the customer's side.

choices.text: The controls became an API on the internet, obeyed by whoever holds a valid key
choices.why: Right. The building stopped mattering; the key became the way in.

choices.text: Cloud storage cannot be encrypted
choices.why: It can, and lesson 11 does it.

choices.text: Physical access by the provider's staff is the larger risk
choices.why: That is still the building, which is the part the course says stopped mattering.

prompt: A request reaches AWS carrying moto's placeholder key `test`. What happens?
hint: The lab's credentials were chosen for this case.

choices.text: AWS refuses it with InvalidClientTokenId, and nothing is created
choices.why: Right. That is why the lab uses a key AWS refuses.

choices.text: AWS runs it against a sandbox account it keeps for tests
choices.why: There is no such account; the request is refused.

choices.text: It is forwarded back to moto
choices.why: AWS knows nothing of your moto.

choices.text: AWS accepts it but charges nothing, since the key is a test key
choices.why: AWS does not accept it at all.

prompt: An inventory script lists networks in `sa-east-1` only, and reports one default VPC. What does lesson 1 say it misses?
hint: Ask every region.

choices.text: Nothing: a default VPC exists only in the account's home region
choices.why: There is one in every region the account has enabled; moto answered with 38.

choices.text: The default VPCs of every other region, each a place to launch a resource
choices.why: Right. One loop over the regions found them all.

choices.text: The subnets of the one VPC it found
choices.why: It found the VPC it was asked about; what it missed is in other regions.

choices.text: The VPCs moto hides from the command line
choices.why: moto hides nothing; the script asked one region.

prompt: After a bucket was public for a day, the policy is removed. Which check proves the exposure is closed, in the way lesson 1 asks?
hint: The fault was found by a request with no credentials.

choices.text: `aws s3api get-bucket-policy` returns an error saying there is no policy
choices.why: That reads one setting. The proof is a stranger's request answered with 403.

choices.text: An anonymous request for an object, answered `403`
choices.why: Right. Ask again as the stranger.

choices.text: A signed request for the same object, answered `200`
choices.why: A signed request is supposed to work; it proves nothing about strangers.

choices.text: The moto terminal shows no error lines
choices.why: A clean log says nothing about what a stranger can read.

prompt: On premises, lesson 1's figure counts how many people who could each say no before stored files reach the internet?
hint: Against one request in the cloud.

prompt: Patients' records leak from a layer the provider runs. According to lesson 2, who answers to the patients under the LGPD?
hint: The responsibility is split; are the consequences?

choices.text: The provider alone, because the failure was below the line
choices.why: The line splits the work, not the consequences: the patients deal with the clinic.

choices.text: The clinic
choices.why: Right. The clinic answers for its patients whoever ran the faulty layer.

choices.text: Nobody, since a shared model means a shared fault
choices.why: Sharing the work does not dissolve the duty to the people in the data.

choices.text: The auditor who certified the provider
choices.why: An attestation describes controls; it takes on no duty towards the clinic's patients.

prompt: Which part of a SOC 2 Type II report is the shared responsibility line written in an auditor's language?
hint: Controls the provider assumes somebody else operates.

choices.text: The scope, listing the services and regions covered
choices.why: The scope says what the auditor examined, not what the customer must do.

choices.text: The opinion at the start of the report
choices.why: The opinion is the verdict on the provider's controls.

choices.text: The complementary user entity controls
choices.why: Right. The report passed on the assumption that you do them.

choices.text: The exceptions, where tested samples failed
choices.why: Exceptions are the provider's failures, not your duties.

prompt: The clinic's account dates from 2021. AWS switched Block Public Access on for new buckets in April 2023. What does lesson 2 conclude about the clinic's oldest buckets?
hint: A default applies from the day it shipped.

choices.text: They kept their old settings; only reading them back tells
choices.why: Right. A default protects the buckets nobody thought about; an inventory finds the ones the change never reached.

choices.text: AWS switched it on for them as well when the default changed
choices.why: The change applied only to buckets created after it.

choices.text: They are safe, since encryption by default arrived in January 2023
choices.why: Encryption at rest says nothing about whether a stranger may read the bucket.

choices.text: They became the provider's responsibility from that date on
choices.why: A default never moves a row across the line; the settings stay yours.

prompt: In the 2023 case of a stolen Microsoft signing key, how was the intrusion found?
hint: A customer's own records.

choices.text: Microsoft's SOC 2 report listed it as an exception
choices.why: A report describes the past, across customers; it found nothing here.

choices.text: A customer changed a setting in its own tenant that blocked the forged tokens before any mail was read
choices.why: No customer setting could have prevented a failure below the line.

choices.text: A customer noticed mail being read in its own audit records and reported it
choices.why: Right. Your own logs are often how anybody learns the provider's half broke.

choices.text: Gartner's forecast predicted the provider's failure
choices.why: The forecast was about customers' failures, and it detects nothing.

prompt: Match each way a provider helps with your half to its example in lesson 2.
hint: Default, guardrail, blueprint.

pairs.right: Block Public Access on for every new bucket
an organisation policy denying regions outside Brazil
AWS Control Tower's landing zone

prompt: Which of these can a clinic check itself, as evidence above the line? Choose all that apply.
hint: If one request reads it back, it is above the line.

choices.text: Whether its bucket has default encryption
choices.why: Right. One request reads it back.

choices.text: Whether the provider's engineers' access to hypervisors is logged
choices.why: Below the line: you read an auditor's report about it.

choices.text: Which ports a security group opens to the internet
choices.why: Right. A setting in your account.

choices.text: Who holds an access key that still works
choices.why: Right. The credential report answers it.

choices.text: Whether the data centre's doors are guarded
choices.why: Physical security is the provider's half, known only through attestations.

prompt: Moving the booking system from a virtual machine to SaaS, which items stay on the clinic's security list?
hint: Every list ends with the same two.

choices.text: Patching the operating system and the network rules
choices.why: Those leave with the machine; on SaaS there is none of yours.

choices.text: The data, and who reaches it
choices.why: Right. No model moves them.

choices.text: Nothing: the vendor secures a SaaS product end to end
choices.why: The vendor secures its platform; the settings inside your tenant are yours.

choices.text: The runtime version the vendor's code asks for
choices.why: That is the vendor's code and the vendor's choice.

prompt: An instance's metadata options show `HttpTokens` as `optional`. Why does lesson 3 treat that as a finding?
hint: The step at the centre of the Capital One case.

choices.text: The machine cannot be reached over SSH until tokens are required, so administrators are locked out
choices.why: Metadata tokens have nothing to do with SSH.

choices.text: The old metadata service still answers a plain request, credentials included
choices.why: Right. IMDSv2 asks for a session token first, which that trick does not get.

choices.text: It means the image is out of date
choices.why: The image's age is a separate question, answered by its description.

choices.text: AWS charges for optional metadata requests
choices.why: There is no such charge; the problem is who can obtain credentials.

prompt: A Lambda function created in 2022 on `python3.7` is still running. What does AWS do about it, according to lesson 3?
hint: The hard case is not the new function.

choices.text: Upgrades it to the current runtime automatically
choices.why: Changing the runtime can break your code, so it is yours to make.

choices.text: Stops it on the day the runtime is deprecated
choices.why: It keeps answering; that is what makes it the hard case.

choices.text: Lets it run unpatched and sends notices to the account's contacts
choices.why: Right. The function keeps answering on a runtime nobody patches.

choices.text: Moves it into a quarantine account
choices.why: There is no such step.

prompt: Match each IaaS question to its PaaS equivalent from lesson 3.
hint: Items change shape, not just number.

pairs.left: which ports are open to the internet
pairs.right: who may invoke the function

pairs.left: which packages the operating system has
pairs.right: which libraries the code ships with

pairs.left: which image the machine was built from
pairs.right: which runtime version the function uses

prompt: A receptionist approved a calendar add-on in 2022 that can still read her whole mailbox. Which item of the SaaS list is that?
hint: Another product that may reach in.

choices.text: Accounts
choices.why: The account is fine; what holds access is a third-party application.

choices.text: Integrations
choices.why: Right. A user granting a third-party application access by clicking allow.

choices.text: Retention of mailbox data
choices.why: Retention is how long records are kept.

choices.text: Sharing outside the company with a link
choices.why: No file was shared; an application was given standing access.

prompt: Under the LGPD, a SaaS vendor that processes personal data on the clinic's behalf, under a data processing agreement, is an ___.
hint: The Portuguese word the law uses.

prompt: Why does lesson 4 say two clouds are not safer than one, the way two locks are?
hint: Add up the exposure, then the defences.

choices.text: The exposure of two environments adds up, and the defences do not cross over
choices.why: Right. A guardrail in one provider's language does nothing in the other.

choices.text: Two providers share one control plane behind the scenes, so a single stolen key opens both of them
choices.why: They share nothing; that is the problem at the seam.

choices.text: Multi-cloud is forbidden by the LGPD
choices.why: The LGPD forbids no architecture.

choices.text: Each provider disables the other's encryption
choices.why: Nothing of the kind happens.

prompt: The credential report shows `reports-sync`'s key last rotated on the day it was created and used every night. What makes it a finding, rather than just a machine's key?
hint: What the report cannot say.

choices.text: Machines are not allowed to hold IAM keys
choices.why: They can; the report alone is not a fault.

choices.text: It never expires, and its owner and storage sit on the other provider
choices.why: Right. Each side sees half and owns none.

choices.text: Nightly use from an address outside AWS proves the key has already leaked to somebody
choices.why: Nightly use is the job doing its work.

choices.text: The policy it carries allows every S3 action
choices.why: It reads one bucket; the policy was narrow.

prompt: A trust policy lets `accounts.google.com` assume a role, with no condition. What does that admit?
hint: Google signs every service account's tokens with the same keys.

choices.text: Only the clinic's own service account
choices.why: Only a condition on `sub` or `aud` pins it to one.

choices.text: Nobody, since a role's trust policy needs an AWS account as its principal
choices.why: A web identity provider is a valid principal for a role.

choices.text: A token from any Google service account in the world
choices.why: Right. The condition is what makes it safe.

choices.text: Any user of the clinic's Google Workspace, but no programs
choices.why: Neither half of that holds; the issuer signs tokens for any service account.

prompt: In lesson 4's capture, the federated session's credentials expired how many hours after the session began?
hint: An `ASIA` key carries an `Expiration`.

prompt: After a VPN joins the office network to the VPC, a security group that allowed `10.0.0.0/8` is left as it was. What changed?
hint: The other side shares the range.

choices.text: Nothing, since the rule itself was not edited
choices.why: The rule is the same; what it admits is not.

choices.text: It now admits every machine on the company network that sits in that range
choices.why: Right. The inside grew.

choices.text: The VPN encrypts traffic, so the rule no longer applies
choices.why: Encryption on the link does not change what the rule admits.

choices.text: AWS narrows the rule to the VPN's addresses automatically
choices.why: Nobody narrows it unless somebody does it on purpose.

prompt: Which statements about hybrid links match lesson 4? Choose all that apply.
hint: A private circuit, a propagated route, a synced leaver.

choices.text: Direct Connect does not encrypt traffic by default
choices.why: Right. Private is not the same as encrypted.

choices.text: Route propagation adds routes to a VPC with no change on the AWS side
choices.why: Right. Routes arrive over BGP.

choices.text: A leaver disabled in the cloud but active on premises returns at the next sync
choices.why: Right. Remove people at the source.

choices.text: A private circuit makes a firewall on the link unnecessary
choices.why: The link is a boundary; treat it as one.

prompt: Someone grants a role on a Google Cloud folder "for convenience". What does lesson 5 say it reaches?
hint: At Google Cloud a grant flows down.

choices.text: Only resources created inside the folder itself, not its projects
choices.why: Projects sit inside folders; the grant reaches them.

choices.text: Every project and resource in it, including future ones
choices.why: Right. Who can read a bucket is found by walking up the hierarchy.

choices.text: Nothing until each project accepts it
choices.why: There is no acceptance step.

choices.text: The organisation and every folder above it
choices.why: Grants flow down, not up.

prompt: A team wants to forbid one engineer from deleting storage. Lesson 5 says that is one line on AWS. What is it usually on Azure?
hint: Azure RBAC is additive.

choices.text: An explicit deny in the engineer's role assignment
choices.why: Customers do not write deny assignments freely.

choices.text: An IAM deny policy on the subscription
choices.why: That is Google Cloud's mechanism.

choices.text: A redesign of the role assignments, or a policy on the configuration
choices.why: Right. Permissions are the union of assignments; you remove the grant or use Azure Policy.

choices.text: Nothing, because Azure denies deletion by default
choices.why: Nothing in Azure denies it by default.

prompt: Why does lesson 5 call an Entra ID Global Administrator an Azure owner in waiting?
hint: A documented switch.

choices.text: Elevate access gives it User Access Administrator at the root of every subscription
choices.why: Right. From there it can grant itself anything.

choices.text: Global Administrators are Owners of every subscription from the start
choices.why: They are not; the two role systems are separate until the switch is used.

choices.text: Azure has a single role system shared by directory and resources
choices.why: It has two, which is why an audit of one misses the other.

choices.text: Subscriptions inherit their owners from the directory's groups
choices.why: Ownership is a role assignment, not an inheritance from groups.

prompt: Match each provider to the setting that keeps storage from going public.
hint: Lesson 5's table.

pairs.right: Block Public Access
`allowBlobPublicAccess` set to false
public access prevention

prompt: At all three providers, which question is answered by default after an incident, and which is not?
hint: The column in the middle.

choices.text: Who read the patients' file is answered; who changed permissions is not
choices.why: The other way round: data access logs are off by default.

choices.text: Neither: nothing is logged until a trail is created
choices.why: Management events are recorded by default at all three.

choices.text: Who changed permissions is; who read the file is not
choices.why: Right. Data access logging is off until somebody turns it on and pays.

choices.text: Both are answered, for 400 days at every provider
choices.why: 400 days is Google Cloud's Admin Activity, and data reads are off by default.

prompt: An SCP denies changing Block Public Access to everyone except `security-admin`. Which account does it leave unprotected?
hint: SCPs flow down, with one exception.

choices.text: Every account in the root OU
choices.why: Attached at the root, it covers the member accounts below.

choices.text: The organisation's management account
choices.why: Right. An SCP never applies there, so it should hold no workloads.

choices.text: Accounts created after the SCP was attached
choices.why: New accounts under the OU inherit it.

choices.text: The `security-admin` role's account, since the role is excepted
choices.why: The exception is a role, not an account; the account stays covered.

prompt: A review must start somewhere in an account with forty users. Which identities does lesson 6 say to look at first?
hint: A permission to change permissions has no ceiling.

choices.text: The ones with the longest policies
choices.why: Length says little. A one-line policy that writes to IAM is worse than a long read-only one.

choices.text: Any identity allowed to write to IAM
choices.why: Right. Whoever can change permissions can grant itself the rest.

choices.text: The users who signed in most recently, since they are the ones who are active today
choices.why: Activity is not the measure of danger; dani's key was dangerous because of what it could write.

choices.text: The users created by contractors
choices.why: Who created a user does not decide what it can do.

prompt: dani's inline policy allowed `iam:AttachUserPolicy` on `"Resource": "*"`, written so she could give analysts the reporting policy. Which change alone would have closed the path, while still letting her do that job, on AWS?
hint: Limit which policy may be attached.

choices.text: Replacing `*` with dani's own user ARN
choices.why: That is the worst choice: it lets her attach anything, to herself only, which is exactly the escalation.

choices.text: Adding MFA to her user
choices.why: Her key signs API requests directly; MFA on the user does not stop it unless a condition demands it.

choices.text: A condition on `iam:PolicyARN` naming the reporting policy only
choices.why: Right. Then "attach the reporting policy" cannot become "attach anything". moto ignores conditions; this is AWS's documented behaviour.

choices.text: Moving the inline policy into a customer managed policy with the very same statements in it
choices.why: The same statements grant the same actions wherever they live.

prompt: Put the steps of closing dani's path in the order lesson 6 gives.
hint: Close the way in before tidying the permissions.
items: run the audit again and read one row
trap: Removing the policies first is the slip: a key that still works can put them back.

prompt: How many actions did the first statement of AWS's compromised-key quarantine policy list, in lesson 6?
hint: Across many services, not only IAM.

prompt: A company federates every person through its identity provider and disables dani there on her last day. Which risk does lesson 6 say is still open?
hint: Disabling stops the next sign-in.

choices.text: Every role session she was issued before that keeps working until it expires
choices.why: Right. That is why sessions should be short, and why AWS documents revoking older sessions.

choices.text: Her IAM user in each account, which federation leaves in place with its password and access key
choices.why: With federation she has no IAM user; that was the point.

choices.text: Her second factor, which stays registered at the identity provider and can still approve a sign-in
choices.why: A factor with no account behind it signs nothing in.

choices.text: Nothing at all, since federation closes every account at once
choices.why: It closes the next sign-in in every account, not the sessions already issued.

prompt: An audit script that matches exact action names reports a clean account. Which of these would it miss, according to lesson 6's list of its limits?
hint: A wildcard that grants the same actions.

choices.text: A user with `AdministratorAccess`
choices.why: The script catches that one: it printed admin's row.

choices.text: An inline policy allowing `iam:Attach*`
choices.why: Right. It grants AttachUserPolicy and prints nothing in a check for the exact string.

choices.text: A user whose access key has not been used for a year and is still active
choices.why: That is the credential report's question, not the policy script's; and it is not a policy it would miss.

choices.text: dani's `iam:AttachUserPolicy` on `*`
choices.why: That is the exact string it looks for; it printed it.

prompt: An access key id starts with `ASIA`. What does that tell a reviewer?
hint: The two prefixes of lesson 7's table.

choices.text: It is a user's long-lived key, with no expiry
choices.why: That is `AKIA`.

choices.text: It belongs to the root user
choices.why: The prefix says nothing about root; it says what kind of credential.

choices.text: A temporary session, which comes with a token and an expiry
choices.why: Right. It stops on its own at `Expiration`.

choices.text: It was created in the São Paulo region, sa-east-1, where the account lives
choices.why: Key ids carry no region.

prompt: caio deletes the commit that added `booking.env` with his key, and force-pushes. Why does lesson 7 say that is not the fix?
hint: Where else is the key now?

choices.text: Because git refuses to forget a commit
choices.why: The point is not git; it is every copy made before the deletion.

choices.text: The key may already be in clones, forks, caches and a scanner's hands; only rotating it makes it worthless
choices.why: Right. Treat it as known to everybody from the moment of the push.

choices.text: Force-pushing can break shared repositories, so it is not allowed
choices.why: Whether allowed or not, it leaves the key valid.

choices.text: AWS needs the commit to find the key and quarantine it
choices.why: Quarantine is a brake from outside; the owner still has to make the key worthless.

prompt: Put the steps of rotating an access key without an outage in order.
hint: Two keys may exist at once.
items: deactivate the old key and watch its last use stop moving
prove the old key is refused
trap: Deleting first is the outage that makes people put rotation off.

prompt: How many access keys may one IAM user hold at once?
hint: The third request said so.

prompt: The booking role's policy allows `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on `"Resource": "*"`. A flaw lets an attacker make the application fetch a secret by a name they choose. What does lesson 7 say that costs?
hint: What else can the role read?

choices.text: Only the booking database's password, since that is the one the code asks for
choices.why: The policy, not the code, sets the limit; and the flaw changes what the code asks for.

choices.text: Every secret in the account
choices.why: Right. The narrow ARN with `-*` keeps it to one on AWS.

choices.text: Nothing, because Secrets Manager checks which program is calling
choices.why: It checks the identity and the policy, not the program.

choices.text: Old versions only, marked `AWSPREVIOUS`
choices.why: The label decides which version, not whether it can be read.

prompt: Why does lesson 7 say the application should fetch the database password from Secrets Manager at run time instead of reading it from an environment variable?
hint: Who else can see the value in each place?

choices.text: Environment variables are limited to 64 characters
choices.why: Length is not the argument; visibility is.

choices.text: Anyone who reads the deployment's configuration reads the variable; a fetch is judged by a policy and recorded
choices.why: Right. What is deployed becomes the secret's name, not its value.

choices.text: A fetched password cannot be read from the program's memory
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: the program still holds it in memory.

choices.text: Secrets Manager rotates it every hour by itself
choices.why: Rotation needs a function somebody writes, or AWS's managed rotation for its own databases.

prompt: A subnet was never associated with any route table. Where do its routes come from?
hint: The detail lesson 8 turns on.

choices.text: It has none, so it can reach nothing at all
choices.why: "No association" is not "no routes".

choices.text: From the VPC's main route table
choices.why: Right. Change the main table and every such subnet changes with it.

choices.text: From the table of the subnet created just before it
choices.why: Creation order plays no part.

choices.text: From its name: a subnet tagged private gets private routes
choices.why: AWS has no field called private; names and tags decide nothing.

prompt: The records database sits in a private subnet with a NAT gateway and accepts connections only from the web subnet. Why does lesson 8 still close its outbound rule?
hint: NAT says nothing about what goes out.

choices.text: A misbehaving process could open a connection out and upload the table; inbound rules never see it
choices.why: Right. Outbound is the direction data leaves in.

choices.text: Because replies to the web servers' queries leave through the outbound rule, which has to name the web subnet for answers to get back
choices.why: Security groups are stateful; replies go out whatever the outbound rules say.

choices.text: NAT gateways also let connections in from the internet, so the outbound rule is what keeps strangers away from the database
choices.why: NAT lets connections out and not in.

choices.text: It saves money
choices.why: Not the argument; the argument is what can leave.

prompt: Which of these are true of an S3 gateway endpoint, as lesson 8 describes it? Choose all that apply.
hint: A route, a prefix list and a policy.

choices.text: It adds a route whose destination is a prefix list
choices.why: Right. The `pl-` id names S3's addresses in the region.

choices.text: Its policy can limit the path to one bucket
choices.why: Right. That is the half that stops data leaving to a thief's bucket.

choices.text: Its `"Principal": "*"` makes the bucket public
choices.why: An endpoint policy only narrows requests already inside the VPC; it grants nothing.

choices.text: It is billed per hour and per gigabyte
choices.why: That is the interface endpoint. The gateway endpoint costs nothing.

choices.text: It gives the subnet a route to the rest of the internet
choices.why: It reaches S3 only; the subnet stays without a route elsewhere.

prompt: SSH on the web servers was open to everybody for a month. The checker proves it was configured. What answers whether anybody actually connected?
hint: Configuration against what happened.

choices.text: A flow log, if it was on before the month began
choices.why: Right. One line per conversation, recorded only if it was already on.

choices.text: Running the checker again, which shows past connections
choices.why: It reads configuration; it never saw a packet.

choices.text: The security group's description field, which AWS updates on each connection
choices.why: Nothing updates it but whoever edits the group.

choices.text: A flow log turned on today, which goes back thirty days
choices.why: Flow logs record from when they are turned on; an account that turns them on after an incident has nothing about it.

prompt: Match each control to what it filters on.
hint: The table of outbound options.

pairs.right: address ranges and ports

pairs.left: a proxy the machines must use
pairs.right: the host name asked for
which names may be resolved
where traffic can go

prompt: A subnet is public when its route table sends `0.0.0.0/0` to an internet ___.
hint: The `igw-` resource.

prompt: Of the four 2017 exposures in lesson 9's table, what pattern does the lesson say is worth keeping?
hint: Whose bucket was it?

choices.text: All four were found by attackers who broke a password
choices.why: No password was broken; the buckets answered researchers as designed.

choices.text: Three of the four were a vendor's bucket holding a customer's data
choices.why: Right. The company in the headline never created the bucket, and its security programme never saw it.

choices.text: Each was caused by a flaw in S3
choices.why: The provider's security held; the setting did what it said.

choices.text: They were all encrypted, which did not help
choices.why: The lesson says nothing about their encryption; it is about grants.

prompt: A bucket ACL grants `READ` to `AuthenticatedUsers`, and an anonymous `curl` is refused with `403`. What does lesson 9 conclude?
hint: Who is in that group?

choices.text: It is private, because the anonymous request was refused
choices.why: That is exactly the false comfort the lesson warns about.

choices.text: It is open to the users of the clinic's own account only
choices.why: The group is everybody with an AWS account, in any organisation.

choices.text: Anybody with any AWS account can read it by signing the request
choices.why: Right. Only reading the access list catches it; a probe without a signature cannot.

choices.text: Nobody can read it until Block Public Access is turned off
choices.why: The bucket had no guardrail in the lesson; and the grant already reaches every AWS account.

prompt: Match each Block Public Access switch to what it does.
hint: Two for new grants, two for existing ones.

pairs.right: refuses a request that would add a public ACL
makes public ACLs already in place grant nothing
refuses a bucket policy that grants public access
limits a public-policy bucket to AWS services and the owner's account

prompt: caio signed a patient's result link with his own IAM user key, valid for seven days, and sent it to the wrong patient. On AWS, what takes that one link back?

choices.why: There is no such list; the bucket never learns a link was made.

choices.text: Taking away the signer's key, or its permission to read the object
choices.why: Right. A link carries the signer's permissions at the moment it is used, which is also why a dedicated signing role is better than a person's key.

choices.text: Editing `X-Amz-Expires` in the address so that it has already run out
choices.why: The patient holds the original address; editing a copy changes nothing they have.

choices.text: Nothing: a signed link works until its expiry whatever happens to the key
choices.why: AWS documents the opposite: deactivating or deleting the signing key stops every link it signed.

prompt: On AWS, at most how many days can a presigned URL signed with an IAM user's long-lived key last?

choices.text: Tenant restrictions refusing sign-in to personal accounts of the same service

choices.text: DLP recognising a CPF number in an upload
choices.why: Right. Content inspection on the way out.

choices.text: Turning off sharing outside the organisation in Google Workspace
choices.why: That is a tenant setting, the first of the three places.

prompt: An object stored with S3's `AES256` sits in a bucket whose policy allows everybody to read. A stranger asks for it. What comes back, and why?

choices.why: S3 decrypts for every request it allows; the stranger got plain text in the lab.

choices.text: The plain text: encryption at rest stops nothing S3 lets through
choices.why: Right. Encryption at rest stops somebody holding the disk, not a request the service answers.

choices.text: A refusal, because encrypted objects never go to anonymous callers
choices.why: That holds for objects under a KMS key, which need a signed request; `AES256` uses S3's own key and has no such rule.

choices.text: An error naming the missing `kms:Decrypt` permission
choices.why: S3's own key involves no KMS permission of yours at all.

prompt: bia holds `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess` and no KMS permission. `clinic-records` encrypts with the clinic's customer managed key. On AWS, what does her `get-object` for a record get?

choices.text: `AccessDenied`: S3 asks KMS to decrypt on her behalf, and KMS refuses

choices.text: The ciphertext of the record as it is stored on disk, which she then cannot read without the key
choices.why: S3 never hands out the stored ciphertext; it decrypts or refuses.

choices.text: The record, because the default key policy delegates to the whole account and everyone in it
choices.why: Delegating to the account hands the decision to IAM, and bia's IAM policies grant no `kms:Decrypt`.

choices.why: Right. A possibly compromised key is a question about who can use it, and the answer is in the policies.

prompt: Put envelope encryption's steps in order, from writing the data to reading it back.

items: ask KMS for a data key, in plain and encrypted form
encrypt the data locally with the plain data key
erase the plain data key from memory
store the encrypted data key beside the encrypted data
send the encrypted data key to KMS to get the plain one back

prompt: Match each word to the question it asks.
hint: Three words, three questions.

pairs.right: in which country is each copy stored?
whose laws can demand access to it?
do you meet the rules, and can you prove it?

right_distractors: how fast can the data be restored?

prompt: An inventory script keeps only the buckets whose region is not `sa-east-1` and is not empty. Which bucket does it miss, and why?
hint: What did `get-bucket-location` print for one of them?

choices.text: None: a bucket's region is always printed in full
choices.why: Not for `us-east-1`, where the answer is `null`.

choices.text: A bucket in `us-east-1`, whose location comes back as `null`, printed `None`
choices.why: Right. The one bucket of patient data abroad is the one whose region reads as nothing.

choices.text: A bucket encrypted with a multi-Region KMS key, which belongs to several regions at once and so has no single one
choices.why: A bucket is always in exactly one region; keys are a separate question.

choices.text: A bucket created by moto, since moto omits the location
choices.why: moto answers as AWS does here; the trap is real.

prompt: The clinic attaches a region-deny SCP to its organisation's root, and its patient data lives in the management account. On AWS, what does the SCP do for that data?
hint: One account is outside every SCP.

choices.text: It refuses every request outside São Paulo, in every account
choices.why: Not in the management account, where SCPs do not apply.

choices.text: Nothing: SCPs bind the member accounts, not the one at the top
choices.why: Right. That is why patient data belongs in a member account.

choices.text: It moves the existing copies back to `sa-east-1`
choices.why: An SCP controls where new requests go; it moves nothing that exists.

choices.text: It blocks IAM too, so nobody can manage users any more
choices.why: The lesson's policy uses `NotAction` to leave the global services out.

prompt: Under the LGPD, the clinic is the controller and AWS an operator. Which of these is the clinic's to answer for?
hint: Lesson 2's line, in legal form.

choices.text: The physical security of the São Paulo data centres
choices.why: That is the operator's half: running its infrastructure as the contract says.

choices.text: A backup bucket of patient data that caio created in Virginia
choices.why: Right. What was put where is the controller's choice, and the transfer needs a ground in article 33.

choices.text: The certificates and audit reports AWS publishes about its own controls, which the clinic relies on
choices.why: Those prove the provider's half; the clinic files them.

choices.text: The hypervisor that separates customers
choices.why: The provider's side of the line.

prompt: Put the three arrangements for EU-US data flows in the order they existed, as lesson 17 tells it.
hint: Two ended in court.
trap: Putting the Privacy Shield last is the slip: Schrems II struck it down in 2020, and the Framework replaced it in 2023.

prompt: The clinic's records sit only in `sa-east-1`, on disks in Brazil, at a United States provider. What does lesson 17 say about a valid United States order for them?
hint: Sovereignty follows the provider as well as the data.

choices.text: It cannot reach them, because residency in Brazil puts them under Brazilian law alone, whatever company holds them
choices.why: Residency settles where the disks are, not whose law reaches the company holding them.

choices.text: They are within reach, since the CLOUD Act covers data in a US provider's control wherever it is stored
choices.why: Right. That is why sovereignty is a fact about a relationship.

choices.text: Only if the data is first copied to a United States region, where American law then applies directly to the disks themselves
choices.why: The CLOUD Act made explicit that location does not decide it.

choices.text: It is blocked by the EU-US Data Privacy Framework
choices.why: That framework concerns EU transfers, and the clinic is not in Europe.
